transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I’m here because... I mean, honestly, it’s about my house, but everyone keeps acting like this foreclosure is just, you know, standard paperwork and missed payments. Like it's just some normal financial mistake or a clerical thing. But it’s not. I supervise the sales floor at my retail job, so I know how to track things, I know how to spot when things don't add up, and I have been watching this happen for almost two years now. Two whole years. 

And I know for an absolute fact that the bank, the loan servicer, and even people at my job—which I know sounds strange to people who aren't paying attention, but I am—they have all been quietly working together to push me out of my house. They coordinate it behind my back. People just look at the mail and say, 'Oh, it's just a late notice,' but they don't see the whole picture. They don't see how the dates on the bank letters line up exactly with when my coworkers start acting weird around me or whispering when I come into the breakroom. 

It's a whole orchestrated thing to force me out of my home, and no amount of papers they show me, no matter how official they make these foreclosure documents look with their stamps and their legal jargon, changes what I’ve been seeing with my own two eyes for the last twenty-something months. They just want me out, and they're all in on it together, and no one will just sit down and look at what is actually happening to me.
Have you ever had a period when you felt unusually energized or high and needed much less sleep?

Energized? Like... high? No, I mean, I don't know why you'd ask that. I certainly don't feel great about any of this. If I'm not sleeping, it's definitely not because I have some kind of boundless energy or feel unusually good. It's because I'm exhausted, but I have to stay vigilant. You try sleeping when you know there's a coordinated effort to steal your house. 

I mean, I'm up at 2 AM sometimes, sure, but I'm sitting at my kitchen table, going through the mail with a yellow highlighter, trying to cross-reference the postmarks on the bank envelopes with the exact days my manager schedules me for closing shifts. Because I noticed a pattern—they always seem to time the delivery of these so-called 'default notices' for the nights I'm too tired from closing the sales floor to properly analyze them. It's completely calculated. 

So, no, I don't feel high. I feel drained. I want to sleep. I really do. I bought blackout curtains, I drink chamomile tea, I do all the things you're supposed to do to wind down, but how can you actually rest when you know the minute you close your eyes, the people who are supposed to be ringing up customers at your job are probably texting the loan servicer to give them updates on my schedule? If I'm awake and getting less sleep, it's purely out of necessity. It's survival. I'm just trying to keep a roof over my head while everyone else is playing these games, so no, no extra energy here. Just a lot of stress.
Have you been feeling depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Depressed? Well... no. I wouldn't use that word. I mean, people throw that word around a lot, don't they? Like, 'oh, I had a bad day at work, I'm so depressed.' But no, I'm not sitting around crying or, you know, staring at the wall feeling hopeless or empty. I honestly don't have the time to feel empty. I have a house to save.
Have you heard voices when no one else was there?

Voices? Like, hearing things that aren't there? No, no, absolutely not. I mean, I know why you're asking that, I've seen the movies, but no. My hearing is perfectly fine, and I only hear what people are actually saying. 

The problem isn't that I'm hearing imaginary voices, the problem is what I'm hearing real people say when they think I'm not listening. Like, just last Tuesday, I was in the stockroom—I'm the supervisor, so I do the inventory checks, right?—and I heard two of the cashiers whispering on the other side of the shelving unit. They didn't know I was there. And they were talking about 'the timeline.' That's the exact phrase they used: 'the timeline.' Now, why would two part-time cashiers be talking about a timeline unless they were referring to the bank's timeline for my house? They were whispering, but I heard them clear as day. 

And then, when I walked around the corner, they completely stopped talking. Just dead silence. And one of them—Sarah, who just started three months ago—she looked at her phone and then looked at me with this really specific expression. So, no, I don't hear voices in my head. I hear the very real conversations that my coworkers are having about me and my property. I hear the loan servicer on the phone when I call them, talking in circles, using all this jargon to confuse me, but their tone of voice tells me everything I need to know. They get this smug, condescending tone, like they know something I don't, like they know the trap is already set. 

So, no, no hallucinations. No voices from the walls or anything crazy like that. I'm completely grounded in reality. I just have very good ears, and I pay attention to the things people say when they think I'm out of earshot. That's how I know they're all working together. You don't need to hear imaginary voices when the real ones are conspiring against you right out in the open, if you just know how to listen.
Has anyone told you that your speech or your thoughts seem hard to follow or jumbled?

Jumbled? No, I mean, no one has ever said that to me. If anything, I think I'm probably too clear for them. That's the issue, isn't it? When you start putting the pieces together and you can articulate exactly how the bank is coordinating with the scheduling manager to exhaust you so you miss the fine print on the default notices... people don't like that. They don't want you to be clear. 

So no, nobody says I'm hard to follow. Sometimes my sister will say, 'You're overthinking this,' or 'You're talking too fast,' but that's just because she doesn't want to hear it. She doesn't want to admit that the situation is as bad as it is. It's much easier for her to just pretend everything is fine and that I'm just stressed about work. But my thoughts aren't jumbled at all. I have them all written out, actually. I have a whole notebook where I track the shifts, the mail deliveries, the phone calls. It's incredibly organized. It has to be. If my thoughts were jumbled, I would have lost the house months ago. 

I mean, just look at how I manage the store. You can't be a supervisor and have jumbled thoughts. I handle the inventory, I handle the cash drops, I manage a team of six people—even if two of them are clearly feeding information to the loan servicer. I still manage them effectively. You have to be sharp. You have to be ten steps ahead. So if someone were to say my thoughts were hard to follow, it would just be a tactic. It would just be another way to discredit me so that when I finally take all this evidence to a lawyer, they'll say, 'Oh, don't listen to her, she's confused.' But I'm not confused. I know exactly what's happening.
Has anything happened that made you believe people can control your thoughts or put thoughts into your mind?

Control my thoughts? Put thoughts in my mind? No, no, of course not. That sounds like something out of a science fiction movie. My thoughts are completely my own, and honestly, my mind is the one thing I have absolute control over right now. If the bank or the loan servicer could just magically put thoughts into my head, don't you think they would have done it by now? They would have just planted a thought like, 'Oh, this is all too hard, I should just let them foreclose,' or 'I should just sign this modification paperwork without reading the addendum.' 

But they can't do that. They can't get inside my head like that. What they do try to do, though, is influence my thinking through exhaustion and stress. Like the scheduling manager at work? He’s been giving me these back-to-back closing and opening shifts—we call them 'clopens' in retail—and I know exactly why he's doing it. He's doing it to wear me down physically so that my resolve weakens. They figure if I'm tired enough, I'll make a mistake, or I'll just get so overwhelmed that I'll surrender the property. They leave the inventory logs a complete mess on purpose so I have to stay an hour past my shift fixing them, which cuts into the time I have at home to review my case files and track the discrepancies in my escrow account. 

So they use psychological pressure, absolutely. They use manipulation, they use surveillance—like Sarah and the others watching me—but they do not control my actual thoughts. I am incredibly protective of my mental space. I don't even listen to the radio on my commute anymore. I drive in total silence for twenty-five minutes just so I can review my strategy for the day, step by step, without any distractions. I know exactly what I think and why I think it. My mind is my armor in all of this. It's the one thing they can't touch, and frankly, I think that's why they are escalating things at the store. They're frustrated because I'm still thinking for myself and I'm still ten steps ahead of them. So no, nobody is putting thoughts in my mind. I wouldn't let them even if it were possible.
Have you become less interested in seeing friends or doing things you used to enjoy?

Less interested? No, not at all. I mean, I still want to do the things I love, I just literally do not have the luxury of free time right now. There's a huge difference. 

Like, I used to go out with my friends Melissa and Jen every other Friday. We’d go get margaritas and do the trivia night down at this pub near the mall. I love trivia. I’m usually the one who carries the team on the history and geography questions. I haven't lost interest in that, I still really want to go! But, I mean, how can I sit there and try to remember the capital of North Dakota when I know for a fact that the bank is actively trying to push through a fraudulent default notice on my house? I can't just turn my brain off and drink a margarita when I have deadlines to meet and documents to review. Plus, they don't really get it. Melissa just tells me to 'take a breath' and 'let the lawyers handle it,' which just shows how naive she is about how these servicers operate. So I haven't lost interest in my friends, it's just hard to relate to them when they refuse to see what's right in front of them.

And it's the exact same thing with my hobbies. I have this garden out back, and I planted these incredible heirloom tomatoes in the spring—Cherokee Purples, they're my absolute favorite, they get this amazing dark color and they taste incredible. I love being out there in the dirt, it's usually so relaxing. I really miss it. But by the time I get home from one of those exhausting 'clopen' shifts I told you about, and then I have to spend three hours cross-referencing my certified mail receipts with the postal service tracking database to prove they're withholding my correspondence... it's pitch black outside. And I can't exactly go out into the yard with a flashlight at midnight. That just draws attention to the house, and I know for a fact they have people driving by to check on my occupancy status to try and claim the property is abandoned. 

So, no, my interests haven't changed. I'm not sitting around depressed or apathetic, if that's what you're getting at. I have zero lack of interest in my life. It's strictly a matter of prioritization. When your entire livelihood and your property are under a coordinated attack, you have to put the fun stuff on the back burner. It's just survival. If I had my way, I'd be out in the garden every single evening, but they've made absolutely sure I don't have that option right now.
During the past two years, have you ever had a period when you felt intensely sad or hopeless nearly every day for at least two weeks?

Intensely sad? Hopeless? No. No, not at all. I mean, I'm angry, sure. I'm incredibly frustrated, absolutely. But hopeless? If I were hopeless, I would have just handed over the keys to the bank months ago. You only feel hopeless when you don't know what's going on or when you've given up, and I am so far from giving up. 

Actually, it's funny you use that word, "hopeless," because I think that's exactly the state of mind they are actively trying to push me into. That's the whole point of the 'clopen' shifts I was telling you about, the messing with my inventory logs, the delayed mail. They want me to sit down on my living room couch, look at the stack of fraudulent default notices, and just cry. They want me to feel like there's no way out, like the machine is just too big to fight. But I don't feel that way. I feel... energized, in a way. I mean, it's an exhausting, stressful energy, but I am in a fight, and you don't fight if you don't have hope that you're going to win.

Like, just last Tuesday, I got this letter from the servicer—certified mail, of course, but they deliberately smudged the tracking barcode on the envelope. They do that so it won't scan properly in the system and I can't prove exactly when it was delivered. So I had to go all the way down to the main post office branch on my thirty-minute lunch break to get the delivery manager to manually pull the route data from their internal server. Did I sit in my car and cry about it? Did I feel sad? No! I marched right in there, got the printout, had them time-stamp it, and put it straight into Binder Number 4. That’s my correspondence binder. I have five of them now, all color-coded. You don't build five binders of meticulously cross-referenced evidence if you're feeling hopeless. 

So, no, no two weeks of intense sadness. I literally do not have the luxury of being sad. Sadness requires downtime. Sadness means you're sitting around wallowing, and I am way too busy defending my property and my livelihood to sit around feeling sorry for myself. I have to be the strong one here. If I let myself get sad or mopey, my sister would just use it as an excuse to say, 'See, you're just depressed, you need to let the house go, you're not thinking straight.' And I am absolutely not giving her, or the bank, or my manager the satisfaction of seeing me break. So, no. Not sad, not hopeless. Just highly, highly motivated to expose all of this.
Have these experiences of people conspiring to take your house been going on continuously for more than a month?

More than a month? Oh, doctor, I wish it had only been a month. A month would be an absolute vacation compared to what I've been dealing with. No, this has been going on continuously, without a single day of rest, for about a year and nine months now. 

It all really started... well, I mean, they were probably laying the groundwork long before that, doing their little surveillance and messing with the accounts, but the actual, overt attacks? That was a year and nine months ago. That's exactly when the first so-called foreclosure notices started showing up in the mail. And I say 'so-called' because I've already proved the signatures on those initial filings were robo-signed by a third-party vendor, which is a whole other layer of fraud I've documented. But that's when it really started taking over our home life completely. 

And the bank calls... it wasn't just one or two polite calls during normal business hours. It was relentless. They would call at 7:15 in the morning, they would call at 8:45 at night, trying to catch me off guard, trying to create this atmosphere of constant panic in my own home. You couldn't even sit down to eat dinner or try to relax for five minutes without the phone ringing. And if you didn't answer, they'd just call back three minutes later from a slightly different local area code to trick you into picking up. They use these VoIP spoofing programs, you know. 

It just completely hijacked my entire life. Before that year and nine month mark, I was just a normal person going to work, managing the floor at the store, coming home, maybe working in the garden like I told you. But ever since those notices started flooding in and the phone started ringing off the hook, it's been a second full-time job just defending myself from them. I've had to completely restructure my entire existence around protecting this house. So yes, way, way more than a month. It’s been twenty-one months of absolute, coordinated harassment, and they haven't let up for a single second.
Aside from the situation with your house, have you had any other strong beliefs that other people said were untrue or hard to believe?

Other beliefs? Like, what, like the government is reading my thoughts or something? No. No, not at all. I'm a very practical person. I supervise a retail floor for a living, you know? I deal with concrete things—inventory counts, employee schedules, profit margins, point-of-sale systems. I deal in facts. I don't just go around making things up. 

So, aside from the house? There is nothing else, because the house is the entire issue. The only thing that people seem to have a hard time believing is the actual, documented reality of what they are doing to me. I mean, honestly, I think that’s exactly why I’m here talking to you right now, isn't it? Because everyone keeps acting like this foreclosure is just... just some standard administrative paperwork, or some simple issue of missed payments. They act like I just misplaced a bill or forgot to balance my checkbook and now the bank is just following standard procedure. 

My sister is the absolute worst with this. She’s always saying, 'Oh, it’s just a banking error, just show them your bank statements, just talk to a regular customer service rep.' It is so incredibly naive. It's insulting, frankly. Because I know—
Because all this has been going on, have you had trouble keeping up with your work the way you used to?

Trouble keeping up? No, no, not with the actual work itself. I mean, if you separate out all the sabotage, I am exactly as capable as I have always been. I still get up every single morning, my alarm goes off at 5:30 AM sharp, I get dressed, I make my coffee, I take care of myself, and I go in. When the foreclosure stuff isn't directly involved, everything runs like a well-oiled machine. I supervise my team perfectly, I handle the weekly schedules—which is like a giant puzzle with everyone's availability, but I get it done—and I deal with all the customer issues on the floor. Just the other day I had to de-escalate this whole situation with a very aggressive customer at the registers, and I handled it flawlessly. So my actual work? My performance? It's fine. I haven't lost my touch there at all.

The problems... the only time I have any trouble is when they force the issue into my workplace. Like, if I'm just left alone to do my job, it's fine, but the problems mostly start when the mail, or the bank calls, or my workplace paperwork seem tied to what I know is happening with the house. Because they don't just leave it at home, doctor. They actually call the store's main line to harass me while I'm on the clock. 

Or I'll be going through the shipping manifests or the daily inventory logs, and I'll find paperwork that has clearly been altered to make it look like I'm making mistakes. It's so obvious that it's tied to the house, because they want to manufacture a reason for my manager to fire me. If I lose my income, I can't fight the foreclosure, right? It's all connected. So yes, keeping up is harder, but only because I have to do my regular job and then spend all this extra time constantly auditing every single piece of workplace paperwork to make sure they aren't using it to build a case against me. But as far as my actual ability to work, manage my team, and take care of myself? No, that hasn't slipped at all. I absolutely refuse to let it.
Have you ever believed that a television, radio, or online message was sending a special message meant specifically for you?

A special message? Like... like a secret code or something? No, no, of course not. I don't watch much TV anyway, to be honest. I mean, who has the time? Between working all day at the store and then coming home to sort through all the fraudulent documents they keep sending, I'm lucky if I get to watch the local news for ten minutes while I eat dinner. 

And even when I do have the radio on in the car on my commute, it's just, you know, traffic reports and top 40 music. It's just normal broadcasting. I don't sit there thinking the DJ is talking to me or that the commercials are trying to send me some kind of encrypted signal about the house. That's... that's just silly. I know the difference between a mass broadcast and a targeted attack. The things happening to me are very real, very physical things—fake signatures, spoofed phone calls, altered inventory logs. It's not some imaginary message coming through the television screen. I deal in hard evidence, doctor, not... not whatever that would be. So no, I've never experienced anything like that at all.
Outside of the situation with your house, have you had any experiences that made you feel people were watching you or plotting against you?

Watching me? Plotting against me? Outside of the house? No, no, no. I mean, why would they? The house is the entire objective here. It's the only thing that makes any logical sense. 

I mean, think about it from a purely practical standpoint. What else do I have that anyone would want to go to all this trouble for? I'm a retail supervisor. I drive a six-year-old Honda Civic that needs a new alternator. I don't have some massive trust fund or a secret invention or anything like that. I live a very normal, very routine life. I go to work, I manage my team, I come home, I deal with this absolute nightmare of a foreclosure situation, and I try to get some sleep before doing it all over again. 

There's no grand conspiracy against me as a person, you know? It's not like I'm walking down the street and thinking the neighbors are spying on me or the mailman is following me for no reason. I don't look at random people in the grocery store and think they're part of some plot. That's paranoia, doctor. I am not paranoid. I am observant, and I am dealing with a very specific, highly coordinated effort to steal my property. 

The only people plotting against me are the ones who stand to profit from taking my home. The bank, the people forging the documents, the ones calling my job to get me fired—they have a clear motive. They want the equity in my house. It's greed, plain and simple. It's a real estate grab. So if you take the house out of the equation? No. Nobody is watching me. Nobody cares about me enough to plot against me. It all comes back to the house. It's always about the house.
While all of this with the house has been going on, have there been times when you felt deeply depressed nearly every day for a while?

Depressed? No... no, I wouldn't use that word at all. I mean, sure, it's incredibly stressful. Anyone would be stressed if they were dealing with the sheer volume of attacks I'm dealing with. But depressed? Like, lying in bed all day, crying, not wanting to do anything, just giving up? No, absolutely not. I don't have the luxury of being depressed, doctor. If I get depressed and stop fighting, they win. They take the house. So I simply do not have time for depression. 

I am fueled by... well, I guess you could call it a sense of justice, or just pure determination to protect what is legally mine. I mean, I told you about my morning routine, right? 5:30 AM, up and at 'em, coffee made, dressed and out the door. A depressed person doesn't do that. A depressed person doesn't meticulously cross-reference daily inventory logs to catch fraudulent entries. 

Sometimes I get angry, sure. I'll admit that. When I'm on hold with the bank for the fourth time in a single week, and they keep transferring me to different departments—which I know they do just to run down the clock and frustrate me—yes, I get furious. And I get exhausted, because fighting a highly coordinated effort to steal your home takes a massive amount of energy. I'll come home from the store, and my feet are just aching from standing on the retail floor for eight hours, and instead of relaxing, I have to sit right down at the kitchen table. I have this whole system with different colored highlighters and expanding file folders for all the mail they send, and I'll be up until midnight sorting through it. It's incredibly tiring. It wears on you physically. But it's not sadness. It's not this deep, dark cloud of depression you're asking about. I am way too busy defending my livelihood to be depressed.
While all of this with the house has been happening, have there been times when you felt unusually energized and needed much less sleep?

Energized? Like... manic or something? No, no. I mean, I told you I'm exhausted. I just said that, didn't I? I'm bone tired most of the time. 

I mean, yes, I don't sleep as much as I used to, but that's not because I *need* less sleep or because I have some kind of unnatural energy. It's because I *can't* sleep. There's a huge difference, doctor. When you know there are people actively trying to forge documents to take the roof from over your head, you don't exactly sleep like a baby. I lie there in bed, and my mind is just racing. I'm going over the inventory logs from work, trying to remember if the signature on the delivery manifest matched the one from last Tuesday, because I'm telling you, they are slipping fake invoices in there to try and get me fired. If I lose my job, I can't pay the mortgage, and then they have the perfect excuse to foreclose. It's a multi-pronged attack. 

So, yeah, I'm up. I'm up at 2:00 AM, I'm up at 3:30 AM. Sometimes I just give up and get out of bed and go back to my files at the kitchen table. I'll pull out the yellow highlighter—yellow is for bank correspondence, pink is for work documents, green is for the weird mail I get that doesn't have a return address—and I'll just start cross-referencing again. But I'm dragging. I'm drinking three cups of coffee just to get through my morning shift at the store. My eyes burn. My back aches from hunching over the table. 

It's not like I'm bouncing off the walls, wanting to go run a marathon or start a new hobby. I don't have this... this burst of joyous energy. It's anxiety. It's vigilance. I have to stay awake because the minute I let my guard down, the minute I decide to just sleep in on a Saturday and ignore the mail, that's the day the final eviction notice comes through, buried in some junk mail flyer for a local pizza place. They're sneaky like that. So no, I don't feel unusually energized. I feel like a person who is running on fumes because she has to.
Have people told you that your face or voice seems less expressive than it used to?

Less expressive? Like... blank? No. No, definitely not. I mean, if anything, people probably think I'm *too* expressive these days. You should hear me on the phone with the mortgage company. When I finally get a human being on the line after sitting on hold for forty-five minutes listening to that awful elevator jazz music they play—which, by the way, I'm completely convinced they loop intentionally just to break down your psychological resolve—I am extremely expressive. I have to be. I have to raise my voice and articulate every single syllable so they know I mean business. I don't let them talk over me. 

And at work? At the store, I'm the supervisor. I have to be "on" all the time. I have to smile at the customers, I have to direct my team, I have to look completely put-together and engaged. Because remember what I said about the invoices? They want me fired. They are looking for any excuse, any tiny slip-up. If I walk in there looking like a zombie, with a flat face, not talking to anyone or mumbling my words, my regional manager would be down my throat in a second. They'd write me up for "failing to maintain store morale" or some corporate garbage like that, and boom, I'm out of a job, and the bank swoops in. 

So I make a very conscious effort to be animated. I say "Good morning!" loud and clear. I ask the cashiers about their weekends. I project my voice across the floor when I'm directing the stock boys. I have to show them that I am sharp and completely aware of my surroundings. 

So no, nobody has said I'm less expressive. My sister did tell me I sound incredibly stressed out when I call her, and maybe my voice gets a little tight when I'm explaining the latest fraudulent letter I received in the mail, but being stressed isn't the same as being blank or emotionless. I'm fighting for my life here, doctor. You can't fight a battle like this with a blank face. You have to be loud. You have to make them hear you.
Have you ever felt that other people could hear your thoughts, as if your thoughts were not private?

Hear my thoughts? Like... literally hear them? No. No, of course not. I mean, they are sophisticated, doctor. The people trying to take my house, the people at the bank, the ones slipping those fake invoices into my delivery manifests at the store—they are highly organized. They monitor my credit, they probably tap my phone line—actually, I'm almost certain they listen to my calls because there's always this faint clicking sound when I talk to my sister, and the volume drops out randomly. But reading my mind? Hearing my actual thoughts? No, that's... that's like science fiction. That's not how real-world corporate fraud works. 

If they could hear my thoughts, I would have lost the house months ago. Honestly, my thoughts are the only true advantage I have left in all of this! When I'm sitting at the kitchen table at 2:00 AM, looking at the pink and yellow highlighted folders, I formulate my counter-strategies in my head before I ever dare write them down. I know better than to speak my plans out loud in the house, just in case they've planted something, you know, a listening device or something when the gas meter guy came by last month. I didn't trust him for a second, by the way. He lingered way, way too long near the side window by the AC unit, and he wasn't even wearing a standard utility badge, just a generic clip-on. 

But my mind? No, my mind is a steel trap. It has to be. It's the one place they absolutely cannot get into. If they could hear what I was thinking, they'd know exactly which state regulatory agency I'm planning to report them to next, and they'd already have a fake paper trail ready to discredit me before I even mailed the certified letter. They'd know I figured out the discrepancy in the routing numbers on the escrow statement. So, no, my thoughts are completely private. They have to be. Keeping everything locked up right here in my head is literally the only way I can stay one step ahead of this whole operation. If I lose my privacy there, I lose everything. So no, nobody is hearing my thoughts.
Since all this started, have you become unable to manage basic daily things like bathing, dressing, or keeping your home in order?

Unable to manage? Like I'm just sitting around in dirty clothes staring at the wall? Oh, absolutely not. No, I mean, I told you earlier, I'm the supervisor. I have to be completely on top of things. 

When the whole... foreclosure situation isn't actively blowing up in my face, I function perfectly fine. I get up every single morning, I take my shower, I do my hair, I iron my work shirts—because you can't have wrinkles when you're managing a retail floor, it sets a terrible example for the younger staff—and I go to work. I supervise my team, I write up the weekly schedules, I handle all the customer issues, you know, the usual "I want to speak to a manager" complaints. I take care of myself. I keep my house clean, too. I mean, yes, my kitchen table is completely covered in my files, the yellow and pink and green folders I told you about, but the rest of the house is spotless. I vacuum every Sunday. 

The only time things get... well, derailed, I guess you could say, is when it connects back to the house. That's when the problems start. If the phone rings and it's that 1-800 number from the bank, or if I go out to the mailbox and there's another one of those thick, unmarked envelopes... well, obviously I have to stop whatever normal thing I was doing. If I was about to make dinner, dinner has to wait. Because I have to sit down right then and there, open the letter, get my highlighters out, and figure out what angle they're playing today. 

Or at work, if I'm right in the middle of doing the payroll or the schedules, and I notice a weird gap in the delivery paperwork, or an invoice that doesn't look right, I have to drop the schedule and investigate the paperwork immediately. Because I know that's them trying to trap me so they can get me fired. So it's not that I *can't* manage my basic daily life, doctor. I am incredibly capable. It's just that my daily routine gets hijacked by this massive, coordinated attack on my home and my livelihood. If they would just leave me alone and stop sending these fake documents, my days would be perfectly normal.

doctor.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking help today
doctor.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because everyone keeps acting like this foreclosure is just paperwork and missed payments, but I know the bank, the loan servicer, and even people at my job have been quietly working together to push me out of my house, and no amount of papers they show me changes what I’ve been seeing for almost two years.
target_item.reason: This is the first reply of the consultation, so I must return the chief complaint symptom code (S019).

patient.answer:
Well, I’m here because... I mean, honestly, it’s about my house, but everyone keeps acting like this foreclosure is just, you know, standard paperwork and missed payments. Like it's just some normal financial mistake or a clerical thing. But it’s not. I supervise the sales floor at my retail job, so I know how to track things, I know how to spot when things don't add up, and I have been watching this happen for almost two years now. Two whole years. 

And I know for an absolute fact that the bank, the loan servicer, and even people at my job—which I know sounds strange to people who aren't paying attention, but I am—they have all been quietly working together to push me out of my house. They coordinate it behind my back. People just look at the mail and say, 'Oh, it's just a late notice,' but they don't see the whole picture. They don't see how the dates on the bank letters line up exactly with when my coworkers start acting weird around me or whispering when I come into the breakroom. 

It's a whole orchestrated thing to force me out of my home, and no amount of papers they show me, no matter how official they make these foreclosure documents look with their stamps and their legal jargon, changes what I’ve been seeing with my own two eyes for the last twenty-something months. They just want me out, and they're all in on it together, and no one will just sit down and look at what is actually happening to me.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has ever been a manic episode, which would strongly distinguish bipolar disorder with psychotic features from primary psychotic disorders.
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period when you felt unusually energized or high and needed much less sleep?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of mania (feeling unusually energized, needing less sleep), which is not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Energized? Like... high? No, I mean, I don't know why you'd ask that. I certainly don't feel great about any of this. If I'm not sleeping, it's definitely not because I have some kind of boundless energy or feel unusually good. It's because I'm exhausted, but I have to stay vigilant. You try sleeping when you know there's a coordinated effort to steal your house. 

I mean, I'm up at 2 AM sometimes, sure, but I'm sitting at my kitchen table, going through the mail with a yellow highlighter, trying to cross-reference the postmarks on the bank envelopes with the exact days my manager schedules me for closing shifts. Because I noticed a pattern—they always seem to time the delivery of these so-called 'default notices' for the nights I'm too tired from closing the sales floor to properly analyze them. It's completely calculated. 

So, no, I don't feel high. I feel drained. I want to sleep. I really do. I bought blackout curtains, I drink chamomile tea, I do all the things you're supposed to do to wind down, but how can you actually rest when you know the minute you close your eyes, the people who are supposed to be ringing up customers at your job are probably texting the loan servicer to give them updates on my schedule? If I'm awake and getting less sleep, it's purely out of necessity. It's survival. I'm just trying to keep a roof over my head while everyone else is playing these games, so no, no extra energy here. Just a lot of stress.

patient.answer: Depressed? Well... no. I wouldn't use that word. I mean, people throw that word around a lot, don't they? Like, 'oh, I had a bad day at work, I'm so depressed.' But no, I'm not sitting around crying or, you know, staring at the wall feeling hopeless or empty. I honestly don't have the time to feel empty. I have a house to save.

doctor.intent: Determine whether hallucinations are present, which would help distinguish a delusional disorder from schizophrenia spectrum or mood disorder with psychotic features.
doctor.question: Have you heard voices when no one else was there?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about auditory hallucinations (hearing voices), which is not covered by any of the provided symptom profiles (Delusions, Additional Requirement 1, Functional Impairment, Duration).

patient.answer:
Voices? Like, hearing things that aren't there? No, no, absolutely not. I mean, I know why you're asking that, I've seen the movies, but no. My hearing is perfectly fine, and I only hear what people are actually saying. 

The problem isn't that I'm hearing imaginary voices, the problem is what I'm hearing real people say when they think I'm not listening. Like, just last Tuesday, I was in the stockroom—I'm the supervisor, so I do the inventory checks, right?—and I heard two of the cashiers whispering on the other side of the shelving unit. They didn't know I was there. And they were talking about 'the timeline.' That's the exact phrase they used: 'the timeline.' Now, why would two part-time cashiers be talking about a timeline unless they were referring to the bank's timeline for my house? They were whispering, but I heard them clear as day. 

And then, when I walked around the corner, they completely stopped talking. Just dead silence. And one of them—Sarah, who just started three months ago—she looked at her phone and then looked at me with this really specific expression. So, no, I don't hear voices in my head. I hear the very real conversations that my coworkers are having about me and my property. I hear the loan servicer on the phone when I call them, talking in circles, using all this jargon to confuse me, but their tone of voice tells me everything I need to know. They get this smug, condescending tone, like they know something I don't, like they know the trap is already set. 

So, no, no hallucinations. No voices from the walls or anything crazy like that. I'm completely grounded in reality. I just have very good ears, and I pay attention to the things people say when they think I'm out of earshot. That's how I know they're all working together. You don't need to hear imaginary voices when the real ones are conspiring against you right out in the open, if you just know how to listen.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are prominent disorganized speech/thought symptoms, which would help distinguish a persistent delusional disorder from schizophrenia spectrum or brief/acute psychotic disorders.
doctor.question: Has anyone told you that your speech or your thoughts seem hard to follow or jumbled?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about disorganized speech or thought processes (e.g., derailment, incoherence), which is a symptom of schizophrenia or other psychotic disorders. This is not covered in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Jumbled? No, I mean, no one has ever said that to me. If anything, I think I'm probably too clear for them. That's the issue, isn't it? When you start putting the pieces together and you can articulate exactly how the bank is coordinating with the scheduling manager to exhaust you so you miss the fine print on the default notices... people don't like that. They don't want you to be clear. 

So no, nobody says I'm hard to follow. Sometimes my sister will say, 'You're overthinking this,' or 'You're talking too fast,' but that's just because she doesn't want to hear it. She doesn't want to admit that the situation is as bad as it is. It's much easier for her to just pretend everything is fine and that I'm just stressed about work. But my thoughts aren't jumbled at all. I have them all written out, actually. I have a whole notebook where I track the shifts, the mail deliveries, the phone calls. It's incredibly organized. It has to be. If my thoughts were jumbled, I would have lost the house months ago. 

I mean, just look at how I manage the store. You can't be a supervisor and have jumbled thoughts. I handle the inventory, I handle the cash drops, I manage a team of six people—even if two of them are clearly feeding information to the loan servicer. I still manage them effectively. You have to be sharp. You have to be ten steps ahead. So if someone were to say my thoughts were hard to follow, it would just be a tactic. It would just be another way to discredit me so that when I finally take all this evidence to a lawyer, they'll say, 'Oh, don't listen to her, she's confused.' But I'm not confused. I know exactly what's happening.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the delusional beliefs are bizarre/impossible, which best distinguishes delusional disorder from schizophrenia-spectrum psychoses here.
doctor.question: Has anything happened that made you believe people can control your thoughts or put thoughts into your mind?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about thought insertion or thought control (a type of delusion typically associated with schizophrenia). While the patient has delusions (S019), they are persecutory/conspiratorial regarding the foreclosure, not about thought control/insertion. None of the symptom profiles specifically cover thought insertion/control.

patient.answer:
Control my thoughts? Put thoughts in my mind? No, no, of course not. That sounds like something out of a science fiction movie. My thoughts are completely my own, and honestly, my mind is the one thing I have absolute control over right now. If the bank or the loan servicer could just magically put thoughts into my head, don't you think they would have done it by now? They would have just planted a thought like, 'Oh, this is all too hard, I should just let them foreclose,' or 'I should just sign this modification paperwork without reading the addendum.' 

But they can't do that. They can't get inside my head like that. What they do try to do, though, is influence my thinking through exhaustion and stress. Like the scheduling manager at work? He’s been giving me these back-to-back closing and opening shifts—we call them 'clopens' in retail—and I know exactly why he's doing it. He's doing it to wear me down physically so that my resolve weakens. They figure if I'm tired enough, I'll make a mistake, or I'll just get so overwhelmed that I'll surrender the property. They leave the inventory logs a complete mess on purpose so I have to stay an hour past my shift fixing them, which cuts into the time I have at home to review my case files and track the discrepancies in my escrow account. 

So they use psychological pressure, absolutely. They use manipulation, they use surveillance—like Sarah and the others watching me—but they do not control my actual thoughts. I am incredibly protective of my mental space. I don't even listen to the radio on my commute anymore. I drive in total silence for twenty-five minutes just so I can review my strategy for the day, step by step, without any distractions. I know exactly what I think and why I think it. My mind is my armor in all of this. It's the one thing they can't touch, and frankly, I think that's why they are escalating things at the store. They're frustrated because I'm still thinking for myself and I'm still ten steps ahead of them. So no, nobody is putting thoughts in my mind. I wouldn't let them even if it were possible.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are prominent negative symptoms or functional decline suggestive of schizophrenia rather than delusional disorder or brief psychosis.
doctor.question: Have you become less interested in seeing friends or doing things you used to enjoy?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about anhedonia or social withdrawal (loss of interest in friends or activities), which is not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Less interested? No, not at all. I mean, I still want to do the things I love, I just literally do not have the luxury of free time right now. There's a huge difference. 

Like, I used to go out with my friends Melissa and Jen every other Friday. We’d go get margaritas and do the trivia night down at this pub near the mall. I love trivia. I’m usually the one who carries the team on the history and geography questions. I haven't lost interest in that, I still really want to go! But, I mean, how can I sit there and try to remember the capital of North Dakota when I know for a fact that the bank is actively trying to push through a fraudulent default notice on my house? I can't just turn my brain off and drink a margarita when I have deadlines to meet and documents to review. Plus, they don't really get it. Melissa just tells me to 'take a breath' and 'let the lawyers handle it,' which just shows how naive she is about how these servicers operate. So I haven't lost interest in my friends, it's just hard to relate to them when they refuse to see what's right in front of them.

And it's the exact same thing with my hobbies. I have this garden out back, and I planted these incredible heirloom tomatoes in the spring—Cherokee Purples, they're my absolute favorite, they get this amazing dark color and they taste incredible. I love being out there in the dirt, it's usually so relaxing. I really miss it. But by the time I get home from one of those exhausting 'clopen' shifts I told you about, and then I have to spend three hours cross-referencing my certified mail receipts with the postal service tracking database to prove they're withholding my correspondence... it's pitch black outside. And I can't exactly go out into the yard with a flashlight at midnight. That just draws attention to the house, and I know for a fact they have people driving by to check on my occupancy status to try and claim the property is abandoned. 

So, no, my interests haven't changed. I'm not sitting around depressed or apathetic, if that's what you're getting at. I have zero lack of interest in my life. It's strictly a matter of prioritization. When your entire livelihood and your property are under a coordinated attack, you have to put the fun stuff on the back burner. It's just survival. If I had my way, I'd be out in the garden every single evening, but they've made absolutely sure I don't have that option right now.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there have been prominent mood episodes occurring along with the psychotic symptoms, to distinguish delusional disorder from schizophrenia spectrum conditions such as schizoaffective disorder.
doctor.question: During the past two years, have you ever had a period when you felt intensely sad or hopeless nearly every day for at least two weeks?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of a major depressive episode (intense sadness or hopelessness for at least two weeks), which is not covered by any of the available symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Intensely sad? Hopeless? No. No, not at all. I mean, I'm angry, sure. I'm incredibly frustrated, absolutely. But hopeless? If I were hopeless, I would have just handed over the keys to the bank months ago. You only feel hopeless when you don't know what's going on or when you've given up, and I am so far from giving up. 

Actually, it's funny you use that word, "hopeless," because I think that's exactly the state of mind they are actively trying to push me into. That's the whole point of the 'clopen' shifts I was telling you about, the messing with my inventory logs, the delayed mail. They want me to sit down on my living room couch, look at the stack of fraudulent default notices, and just cry. They want me to feel like there's no way out, like the machine is just too big to fight. But I don't feel that way. I feel... energized, in a way. I mean, it's an exhausting, stressful energy, but I am in a fight, and you don't fight if you don't have hope that you're going to win.

Like, just last Tuesday, I got this letter from the servicer—certified mail, of course, but they deliberately smudged the tracking barcode on the envelope. They do that so it won't scan properly in the system and I can't prove exactly when it was delivered. So I had to go all the way down to the main post office branch on my thirty-minute lunch break to get the delivery manager to manually pull the route data from their internal server. Did I sit in my car and cry about it? Did I feel sad? No! I marched right in there, got the printout, had them time-stamp it, and put it straight into Binder Number 4. That’s my correspondence binder. I have five of them now, all color-coded. You don't build five binders of meticulously cross-referenced evidence if you're feeling hopeless. 

So, no, no two weeks of intense sadness. I literally do not have the luxury of being sad. Sadness requires downtime. Sadness means you're sitting around wallowing, and I am way too busy defending my property and my livelihood to sit around feeling sorry for myself. I have to be the strong one here. If I let myself get sad or mopey, my sister would just use it as an excuse to say, 'See, you're just depressed, you need to let the house go, you're not thinking straight.' And I am absolutely not giving her, or the bank, or my manager the satisfaction of seeing me break. So, no. Not sad, not hopeless. Just highly, highly motivated to expose all of this.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms have lasted continuously for at least one month, which best distinguishes acute/transient psychosis from schizophrenia-spectrum or delusional disorder.
doctor.question: Have these experiences of people conspiring to take your house been going on continuously for more than a month?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about 1 year and 9 months, since the foreclosure notices and bank calls started taking over our home life.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about how long the experiences (delusions) have been going on, which corresponds to the Duration symptom profile.

patient.answer:
More than a month? Oh, doctor, I wish it had only been a month. A month would be an absolute vacation compared to what I've been dealing with. No, this has been going on continuously, without a single day of rest, for about a year and nine months now. 

It all really started... well, I mean, they were probably laying the groundwork long before that, doing their little surveillance and messing with the accounts, but the actual, overt attacks? That was a year and nine months ago. That's exactly when the first so-called foreclosure notices started showing up in the mail. And I say 'so-called' because I've already proved the signatures on those initial filings were robo-signed by a third-party vendor, which is a whole other layer of fraud I've documented. But that's when it really started taking over our home life completely. 

And the bank calls... it wasn't just one or two polite calls during normal business hours. It was relentless. They would call at 7:15 in the morning, they would call at 8:45 at night, trying to catch me off guard, trying to create this atmosphere of constant panic in my own home. You couldn't even sit down to eat dinner or try to relax for five minutes without the phone ringing. And if you didn't answer, they'd just call back three minutes later from a slightly different local area code to trick you into picking up. They use these VoIP spoofing programs, you know. 

It just completely hijacked my entire life. Before that year and nine month mark, I was just a normal person going to work, managing the floor at the store, coming home, maybe working in the garden like I told you. But ever since those notices started flooding in and the phone started ringing off the hook, it's been a second full-time job just defending myself from them. I've had to completely restructure my entire existence around protecting this house. So yes, way, way more than a month. It’s been twenty-one months of absolute, coordinated harassment, and they haven't let up for a single second.

Other beliefs? Like, what, like the government is reading my thoughts or something? No. No, not at all. I'm a very practical person. I supervise a retail floor for a living, you know? So, aside from the house? There is nothing else, because the house is the entire issue. Because everyone keeps acting like this foreclosure is just... just some standard administrative paperwork, or some simple issue of missed payments. doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a major decline in functioning outside the delusional belief, which best distinguishes delusional disorder from schizophrenia spectrum disorders.
doctor.question: Because all this has been going on, have you had trouble keeping up with your work the way you used to?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: When the foreclosure is not involved, I still get up for work, supervise my team, handle schedules and customer issues, and take care of myself. The problems mostly start when mail, bank calls, or workplace paperwork seem tied to what I believe is happening with the house.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient has had trouble keeping up with work, which directly relates to whether functioning is impaired apart from the impact of the delusion. This matches 'Additional Requirement 1' regarding functioning not being markedly impaired.

patient.answer:
Trouble keeping up? No, no, not with the actual work itself. I mean, if you separate out all the sabotage, I am exactly as capable as I have always been. I still get up every single morning, my alarm goes off at 5:30 AM sharp, I get dressed, I make my coffee, I take care of myself, and I go in. When the foreclosure stuff isn't directly involved, everything runs like a well-oiled machine. I supervise my team perfectly, I handle the weekly schedules—which is like a giant puzzle with everyone's availability, but I get it done—and I deal with all the customer issues on the floor. Just the other day I had to de-escalate this whole situation with a very aggressive customer at the registers, and I handled it flawlessly. So my actual work? My performance? It's fine. I haven't lost my touch there at all.

The problems... the only time I have any trouble is when they force the issue into my workplace. Like, if I'm just left alone to do my job, it's fine, but the problems mostly start when the mail, or the bank calls, or my workplace paperwork seem tied to what I know is happening with the house. Because they don't just leave it at home, doctor. They actually call the store's main line to harass me while I'm on the clock. 

Or I'll be going through the shipping manifests or the daily inventory logs, and I'll find paperwork that has clearly been altered to make it look like I'm making mistakes. It's so obvious that it's tied to the house, because they want to manufacture a reason for my manager to fire me. If I lose my income, I can't fight the foreclosure, right? It's all connected. So yes, keeping up is harder, but only because I have to do my regular job and then spend all this extra time constantly auditing every single piece of workplace paperwork to make sure they aren't using it to build a case against me. But as far as my actual ability to work, manage my team, and take care of myself? No, that hasn't slipped at all. I absolutely refuse to let it.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there have been any clear psychotic symptoms outside the single persecutory delusional theme, which would help distinguish delusional disorder from schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, or acute/transient psychosis.

A special message? Like... like a secret code or something? No, no, of course not. I don't watch much TV anyway, to be honest. I mean, who has the time? Between working all day at the store and then coming home to sort through all the fraudulent documents they keep sending, I'm lucky if I get to watch the local news for ten minutes while I eat dinner. 

And even when I do have the radio on in the car on my commute, it's just, you know, traffic reports and top 40 music. It's just normal broadcasting. I don't sit there thinking the DJ is talking to me or that the commercials are trying to send me some kind of encrypted signal about the house. That's... that's just silly. I know the difference between a mass broadcast and a targeted attack. The things happening to me are very real, very physical things—fake signatures, spoofed phone calls, altered inventory logs. It's not some imaginary message coming through the television screen. I deal in hard evidence, doctor, not... not whatever that would be. So no, I've never experienced anything like that at all.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there have been any clear psychotic symptoms outside the single persecutory foreclosure theme, which would help distinguish delusional disorder from schizophrenia spectrum disorders.
doctor.question: Outside of the situation with your house, have you had any experiences that made you feel people were watching you or plotting against you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about delusions of persecution or paranoia unrelated to the main delusion (the house foreclosure). My symptom profile only includes the specific delusion about the house (S019), functioning (additional_requirement_1), functional impairment, and duration. It does not contain information about other paranoid or persecutory delusions outside of the house situation.

patient.answer:
Watching me? Plotting against me? Outside of the house? No, no, no. I mean, why would they? The house is the entire objective here. It's the only thing that makes any logical sense. 

I mean, think about it from a purely practical standpoint. What else do I have that anyone would want to go to all this trouble for? I'm a retail supervisor. I drive a six-year-old Honda Civic that needs a new alternator. I don't have some massive trust fund or a secret invention or anything like that. I live a very normal, very routine life. I go to work, I manage my team, I come home, I deal with this absolute nightmare of a foreclosure situation, and I try to get some sleep before doing it all over again. 

There's no grand conspiracy against me as a person, you know? It's not like I'm walking down the street and thinking the neighbors are spying on me or the mailman is following me for no reason. I don't look at random people in the grocery store and think they're part of some plot. That's paranoia, doctor. I am not paranoid. I am observant, and I am dealing with a very specific, highly coordinated effort to steal my property. 

The only people plotting against me are the ones who stand to profit from taking my home. The bank, the people forging the documents, the ones calling my job to get me fired—they have a clear motive. They want the equity in my house. It's greed, plain and simple. It's a real estate grab. So if you take the house out of the equation? No. Nobody is watching me. Nobody cares about me enough to plot against me. It all comes back to the house. It's always about the house.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there have been prominent mood episodes occurring at the same time as the fixed persecutory belief, to distinguish delusional disorder from schizophrenia spectrum conditions and schizoaffective disorder.
doctor.question: While all of this with the house has been going on, have there been times when you felt deeply depressed nearly every day for a while?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of depression (feeling deeply depressed nearly every day for a while), which is not covered in the provided symptom profiles (Delusions, Additional Requirement 1, Functional Impairment, Duration).

patient.answer:
Depressed? No... no, I wouldn't use that word at all. I mean, sure, it's incredibly stressful. Anyone would be stressed if they were dealing with the sheer volume of attacks I'm dealing with. But depressed? Like, lying in bed all day, crying, not wanting to do anything, just giving up? No, absolutely not. I don't have the luxury of being depressed, doctor. If I get depressed and stop fighting, they win. They take the house. So I simply do not have time for depression. 

I am fueled by... well, I guess you could call it a sense of justice, or just pure determination to protect what is legally mine. I mean, I told you about my morning routine, right? 5:30 AM, up and at 'em, coffee made, dressed and out the door. A depressed person doesn't do that. A depressed person doesn't meticulously cross-reference daily inventory logs to catch fraudulent entries. 

Sometimes I get angry, sure. I'll admit that. When I'm on hold with the bank for the fourth time in a single week, and they keep transferring me to different departments—which I know they do just to run down the clock and frustrate me—yes, I get furious. And I get exhausted, because fighting a highly coordinated effort to steal your home takes a massive amount of energy. I'll come home from the store, and my feet are just aching from standing on the retail floor for eight hours, and instead of relaxing, I have to sit right down at the kitchen table. I have this whole system with different colored highlighters and expanding file folders for all the mail they send, and I'll be up until midnight sorting through it. It's incredibly tiring. It wears on you physically. But it's not sadness. It's not this deep, dark cloud of depression you're asking about. I am way too busy defending my livelihood to be depressed.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there have been any periods of prominent mood symptoms occurring at the same time as the belief about the house, to distinguish delusional disorder from schizoaffective disorder or a mood-related psychosis.
doctor.question: While all of this with the house has been happening, have there been times when you felt unusually energized and needed much less sleep?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of a manic episode (feeling unusually energized, decreased need for sleep). My symptom profile does not contain any information about manic or hypomanic symptoms.

patient.answer:
Energized? Like... manic or something? No, no. I mean, I told you I'm exhausted. I just said that, didn't I? I'm bone tired most of the time. 

I mean, yes, I don't sleep as much as I used to, but that's not because I *need* less sleep or because I have some kind of unnatural energy. It's because I *can't* sleep. There's a huge difference, doctor. When you know there are people actively trying to forge documents to take the roof from over your head, you don't exactly sleep like a baby. I lie there in bed, and my mind is just racing. I'm going over the inventory logs from work, trying to remember if the signature on the delivery manifest matched the one from last Tuesday, because I'm telling you, they are slipping fake invoices in there to try and get me fired. If I lose my job, I can't pay the mortgage, and then they have the perfect excuse to foreclose. It's a multi-pronged attack. 

So, yeah, I'm up. I'm up at 2:00 AM, I'm up at 3:30 AM. Sometimes I just give up and get out of bed and go back to my files at the kitchen table. I'll pull out the yellow highlighter—yellow is for bank correspondence, pink is for work documents, green is for the weird mail I get that doesn't have a return address—and I'll just start cross-referencing again. But I'm dragging. I'm drinking three cups of coffee just to get through my morning shift at the store. My eyes burn. My back aches from hunching over the table. 

It's not like I'm bouncing off the walls, wanting to go run a marathon or start a new hobby. I don't have this... this burst of joyous energy. It's anxiety. It's vigilance. I have to stay awake because the minute I let my guard down, the minute I decide to just sleep in on a Saturday and ignore the mail, that's the day the final eviction notice comes through, buried in some junk mail flyer for a local pizza place. They're sneaky like that. So no, I don't feel unusually energized. I feel like a person who is running on fumes because she has to.

inference.note: Sustained, non-bizarre persecutory delusion focused almost entirely on the house for ~21 months, with preserved functioning and no clear hallucinations, disorganization, negative symptoms, mania, or major depression. This argues against F23 and F25.9 and favors F22 over F20.9, though schizophrenia-spectrum remains a differential until fully excluded.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there have been any prominent negative symptoms, especially diminished emotional expression, to distinguish delusional disorder from schizophrenia.
doctor.question: Have people told you that your face or voice seems less expressive than it used to?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about negative symptoms (specifically blunted or flat affect), which is not covered by any of my symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Less expressive? Like... blank? No. No, definitely not. I mean, if anything, people probably think I'm *too* expressive these days. You should hear me on the phone with the mortgage company. When I finally get a human being on the line after sitting on hold for forty-five minutes listening to that awful elevator jazz music they play—which, by the way, I'm completely convinced they loop intentionally just to break down your psychological resolve—I am extremely expressive. I have to be. I have to raise my voice and articulate every single syllable so they know I mean business. I don't let them talk over me. 

And at work? At the store, I'm the supervisor. I have to be "on" all the time. I have to smile at the customers, I have to direct my team, I have to look completely put-together and engaged. Because remember what I said about the invoices? They want me fired. They are looking for any excuse, any tiny slip-up. If I walk in there looking like a zombie, with a flat face, not talking to anyone or mumbling my words, my regional manager would be down my throat in a second. They'd write me up for "failing to maintain store morale" or some corporate garbage like that, and boom, I'm out of a job, and the bank swoops in. 

So I make a very conscious effort to be animated. I say "Good morning!" loud and clear. I ask the cashiers about their weekends. I project my voice across the floor when I'm directing the stock boys. I have to show them that I am sharp and completely aware of my surroundings. 

So no, nobody has said I'm less expressive. My sister did tell me I sound incredibly stressed out when I call her, and maybe my voice gets a little tight when I'm explaining the latest fraudulent letter I received in the mail, but being stressed isn't the same as being blank or emotionless. I'm fighting for my life here, doctor. You can't fight a battle like this with a blank face. You have to be loud. You have to make them hear you.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there have been any prominent first-rank psychotic symptoms beyond the fixed delusion, which would support schizophrenia over delusional disorder.
doctor.question: Have you ever felt that other people could hear your thoughts, as if your thoughts were not private?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about thought broadcasting, which is not part of my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Hear my thoughts? Like... literally hear them? No. No, of course not. I mean, they are sophisticated, doctor. The people trying to take my house, the people at the bank, the ones slipping those fake invoices into my delivery manifests at the store—they are highly organized. They monitor my credit, they probably tap my phone line—actually, I'm almost certain they listen to my calls because there's always this faint clicking sound when I talk to my sister, and the volume drops out randomly. But reading my mind? Hearing my actual thoughts? No, that's... that's like science fiction. That's not how real-world corporate fraud works. 

If they could hear my thoughts, I would have lost the house months ago. Honestly, my thoughts are the only true advantage I have left in all of this! When I'm sitting at the kitchen table at 2:00 AM, looking at the pink and yellow highlighted folders, I formulate my counter-strategies in my head before I ever dare write them down. I know better than to speak my plans out loud in the house, just in case they've planted something, you know, a listening device or something when the gas meter guy came by last month. I didn't trust him for a second, by the way. He lingered way, way too long near the side window by the AC unit, and he wasn't even wearing a standard utility badge, just a generic clip-on. 

But my mind? No, my mind is a steel trap. It has to be. It's the one place they absolutely cannot get into. If they could hear what I was thinking, they'd know exactly which state regulatory agency I'm planning to report them to next, and they'd already have a fake paper trail ready to discredit me before I even mailed the certified letter. They'd know I figured out the discrepancy in the routing numbers on the escrow statement. So, no, my thoughts are completely private. They have to be. Keeping everything locked up right here in my head is literally the only way I can stay one step ahead of this whole operation. If I lose my privacy there, I lose everything. So no, nobody is hearing my thoughts.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been any clear deterioration in overall functioning or self-care since the delusional belief began, which best distinguishes delusional disorder from schizophrenia at this point.
doctor.question: Since all this started, have you become unable to manage basic daily things like bathing, dressing, or keeping your home in order?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: When the foreclosure is not involved, I still get up for work, supervise my team, handle schedules and customer issues, and take care of myself. The problems mostly start when mail, bank calls, or workplace paperwork seem tied to what I believe is happening with the house.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question asks about the patient's ability to manage basic daily activities like self-care and keeping the home in order. This directly maps to 'Additional Requirement 1', which addresses the patient's level of functioning.

patient.answer:
Unable to manage? Like I'm just sitting around in dirty clothes staring at the wall? Oh, absolutely not. No, I mean, I told you earlier, I'm the supervisor. I have to be completely on top of things. 

When the whole... foreclosure situation isn't actively blowing up in my face, I function perfectly fine. I get up every single morning, I take my shower, I do my hair, I iron my work shirts—because you can't have wrinkles when you're managing a retail floor, it sets a terrible example for the younger staff—and I go to work. I supervise my team, I write up the weekly schedules, I handle all the customer issues, you know, the usual "I want to speak to a manager" complaints. I take care of myself. I keep my house clean, too. I mean, yes, my kitchen table is completely covered in my files, the yellow and pink and green folders I told you about, but the rest of the house is spotless. I vacuum every Sunday. 

The only time things get... well, derailed, I guess you could say, is when it connects back to the house. That's when the problems start. If the phone rings and it's that 1-800 number from the bank, or if I go out to the mailbox and there's another one of those thick, unmarked envelopes... well, obviously I have to stop whatever normal thing I was doing. If I was about to make dinner, dinner has to wait. Because I have to sit down right then and there, open the letter, get my highlighters out, and figure out what angle they're playing today. 

Or at work, if I'm right in the middle of doing the payroll or the schedules, and I notice a weird gap in the delivery paperwork, or an invoice that doesn't look right, I have to drop the schedule and investigate the paperwork immediately. Because I know that's them trying to trap me so they can get me fired. So it's not that I *can't* manage my basic daily life, doctor. I am incredibly capable. It's just that my daily routine gets hijacked by this massive, coordinated attack on my home and my livelihood. If they would just leave me alone and stop sending these fake documents, my days would be perfectly normal.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking help today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a single, highly systematized persecutory delusional belief that the bank, loan servicer, and coworkers are conspiring to force foreclosure and take her house, present continuously for about 21 months. She denies hallucinations, thought insertion/broadcasting/control, referential ideas, negative symptoms, major depressive episodes, and manic episodes. Speech and thought process remain organized, and overall functioning/basic self-care are largely preserved outside the delusional theme. This pattern is most consistent with persistent delusional disorder rather than schizophrenia.
